query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) as an alloying element (e.g. around 5–10 wt% relative to the other constituents) to the baseline high-entropy alloy composition will improve its mechanical durability, reduce room‐temperature creep deformation, and enhance its corrosion resistance, compared to the untreated (Mo-free) alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy formulated for aerospace fasteners (e.g. a Cr25Co25Ni25Fe25-based HEA) in its cast or consolidated as-cast state without Mo.
generation.intervention: Introduce Mo into the HEA composition by alloying a targeted 5–10 wt% Mo during melting and casting (or powder metallurgy), so that the final alloy contains the Mo additive uniformly dispersed throughout the matrix.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under standard casting or consolidation techniques and then tested at room temperature. Mechanical tests (tensile and nanoindentation creep tests) are conducted at room temperature and corrosion resistance is evaluated using potentiodynamic polarization in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo atoms are expected to induce lattice distortions and promote the formation of a more stable local chemical order; they also participate in forming stronger Mo–O bonds in the surface oxide. These effects hinder dislocation motion and slow atomic diffusion, thereby improving resistance to creep and corrosion.
generation.mechanism: Mo addition leads to a solution strengthening effect that raises the yield and ultimate tensile strengths by hindering dislocation motion. Simultaneously, the presence of Mo helps stabilize the alloy’s microstructure against room-temperature creep by reducing atomic mobility, and it fosters a more protective, corrosion-resistant oxide layer through the formation of Mo-rich compounds at the surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the Mo-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength and improved mechanical durability, reduced room-temperature creep displacement, and a higher corrosion potential with lower corrosion current density in a saline environment. The magnitude of these improvements is suggested by prior work to be on the order of a 20–30% increase in strength, although the exact values remain uncertain.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without any Mo addition used in aerospace fastener applications.
generation.boundary: It is assumed that all other alloying elements, processing routes, and testing conditions remain the same as in the baseline material preparation.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports improvements in mechanical and corrosion properties with Mo addition, the precise quantitative impact on room-temperature creep resistance and the combined effect when targeting aerospace fastener applications remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the baseline HEA composition and the other with an identical composition except with an intentional addition of 5–10 wt% Mo. Process both sets under the same casting or powder metallurgy conditions. Subject the samples to room temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength and ductility, perform nanoindentation creep experiments at room temperature to measure creep displacement under a standard load, and conduct potentiodynamic polarization tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution to obtain corrosion potential and current density.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Nanoindentation-measured creep displacement and creep rate at room temperature
Corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (Icorr) from potentiodynamic polarization tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Mo-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical durability (i.e., higher yield strength), a measurable reduction in creep displacement under the same loading conditions, and an enhanced corrosion performance (higher Ecorr and lower Icorr) compared to the baseline alloy.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
